source.title: Computational Tradeoffs in Image Synthesis: Diffusion, Masked-Token, and Next-Token Prediction
source.authors: Maciej Kilian; Varun Jampani; Luke S. Zettlemoyer

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends scaling analysis to transformer-based image synthesis and reports its own loss trends across training compute.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling laws, but cited results are not rows. Its own relevant measurement is final training loss plotted against training compute (Figure 4); the authors state that objectives show predictable trends. They explicitly use final train loss in an infinite-data regime, and say the losses are not comparable across objectives. The paper does not report fitted power-law exponents or a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. CLIP and FID results are not rows for these loss-based versions.
record.test_reason: The study trains image-synthesis transformers over a grid of sizes and data amounts. It plots its own final training loss against compute (Figure 4) and states that all objectives follow predictable scaling trends like past work. This bears on V5 (image models), but only qualitatively: no power law is fitted and no exponents are given.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors' headline conclusions are about FID/CLIP and inference efficiency. Token methods, led by next-token prediction, give better prompt following. Next-token prediction leads on FID at low compute, but diffusion eventually matches it. Next-token prediction is most inference-efficient. On loss, they only state that final train loss follows predictable scaling trends similar to prior work.
record.recipe_differences: This is an image-synthesis scaling study, not a reproduction of the language-model loss-fitting or compute-optimal-allocation methods; it plots final training loss against compute without reporting fitted exponents or allocation laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Training objective, model size, dataset size, and autoencoder setup are varied, but the paper does not report fitted-law sensitivity to these choices.

fits_no_version.finding: On FID and CLIP against training compute, next-token prediction is more compute-efficient early, but the trends suggest diffusion eventually matches it on FID. Smaller models trained longer often surpass larger ones.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Perceptual-quality metrics of image generators scale with compute, with crossovers between training objectives and a compute-optimal split that favours smaller models trained longer.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 4 (right) shows that the loss scale of diffusion models differs with the autoencoder used.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss scaling curves in latent generative models shift with the choice of latent space or tokenizer.

record.problems: The relevant loss results are shown in a figure without numerical values in the supplied text; no uncertainty estimates, fitted exponents, or explicit power-law goodness-of-fit results are reported. Losses across objectives are explicitly not compared.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3 reports FID and CLIP performance, not the loss measures named by the tested version. Figure 2 and the autoencoder discussion report reconstruction/perceptual metrics rather than the relevant scaling-law result.

untested.parts: Only latent image-synthesis pretraining at 256x256 is covered. No fitted power-law exponents or goodness-of-fit. No video or other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
Not tested: no extrapolation from small fits.
Not tested for loss. The only allocation remark is on perceptual metrics.
Downstream tasks are explicitly out of scope.
Not tested: no exponents or fitting choices compared.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's limits_scope label is replaced by supports. A missing fit is an untested part of V5, not a qualifying result. Researchers should weigh this as weak, qualitative evidence: the loss values are figure-only and no power law is fitted.

versions.untested_parts: The study concerns image synthesis, not held-out language-model pretraining loss.
It does not fit laws on small runs and test predictions on runs orders of magnitude larger.
It does not determine a loss-minimising parameter/token split at fixed compute or fit growth trends for that split.
It does not test how depth, width, or architecture details affect loss at fixed parameter count.
Tests image synthesis pretraining only. It does not test other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, transfer, held-out loss, or explicitly fit and compare power-law forms.
The authors state that downstream-task utility is outside the study's scope.
It does not report how fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations change with fitting choices, nor evidence that curves bend away from a single power law.

rows.note: The text says the objectives follow predictable scaling trends and describes their trends as similar to prior work. The figure's numerical values and fitted exponents are not given in the text.
rows.check: Partial is the wrong state: the authors report the trend as present, not weaker. The evidence is qualitative (figure plus authors' words: 'All objectives follow predictable scaling trends'), with no fitted power law. It is final train loss in an infinite-data regime, so it stands in for held-out loss. Constant learning-rate schedule, with checkpoints reused as dataset sizes.

relationships.condition: Transformer latent image synthesis (diffusion, next-token, masked-token), S–XL, 256x256 web image-text data
relationships.reason: The authors state that final training loss for all three objectives follows predictable compute-scaling trends similar to prior work (r1–r3). The support is qualitative and figure-only, with no fitted exponents.
relationships.display_finding: Final training loss showed predictable compute-scaling trends for diffusion, next-token prediction and masked-token prediction, although the evidence was qualitative and exponents were not fitted.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
